opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think "world model" has become one of those terms where everyone means something slightly different, so it helps to separate out a few forms.

The way I see it, a world model is fundamentally a system that can predict how the world evolves, especially in response to actions. If you have a current state and you take an action, what happens next? That's the core capability. But the form it takes can vary a lot.

One form is the video-based world model. You generate future frames, pixels, conditioned on the past and on some action or prompt. That's very intuitive because humans perceive the world visually, and video carries a huge amount of information about physics, about geometry, about how objects interact. A lot of the work we've done on physical AI goes in this direction, where you train on large amounts of video so the model learns things like gravity, collisions, how a robot arm moves through a scene.

Another form works in a latent space. Instead of predicting every pixel, you predict a compressed representation of the future. The argument there is efficiency: you don't need to render every leaf on a tree to know that the car in front of you is going to brake. For planning and control, a good latent representation may be enough, and it's much cheaper.

Then there are more explicit, structured forms: 3D representations, simulators, physics engines. Traditional simulation is a world model too. It's hand-built rather than learned, and it's very accurate within its assumptions, but it's hard to scale to the full diversity of the real world. A lot of interesting work right now is about combining the two, using learned models to fill in what simulators can't capture and using structure to make learned models more consistent.

And you could even argue language models carry a kind of world model, an abstract, symbolic one. They know that if you drop a glass it will probably break. But that knowledge isn't grounded in physics at the level a robot needs to actually manipulate that glass.

So I don't think one form will simply win. Different applications need different levels of fidelity and abstraction. For training physical AI, robots, autonomous vehicles, you need something grounded in the physical world, ideally something you can interact with, so the AI can practice and fail safely before going into reality. That's why I think of world models as the key piece for physical AI: they let you generate experience, not just data. And over time I expect these forms to converge, with models that can render pixels when you need them, reason in latent space when that's sufficient, and keep consistency with 3D and physics underneath.

r001.rationale: The response says different applications need different levels of fidelity and abstraction, and connects video, latent, and structured models to distinct needs such as planning, control, and physical AI training.

r002.rationale: It describes several representations of world models, but does not characterize them as descriptions of the same underlying world through different observations.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I think about it, a world model is fundamentally a simulator — something that, given the current state of the world and an action, can predict what the world will look like next. That's the core definition. But the forms it can take vary quite a bit depending on what you're trying to do with it.

The first form, and probably the most visible one right now, is the generative video model. You give it a text prompt or an image, maybe a camera trajectory or a control signal, and it generates a video of what happens. That's a world model in the sense that it has learned the physics, the dynamics, the appearance of the world well enough to render a plausible future. Cosmos is in this family. The appeal is that video is a very rich, very general representation — you can observe almost everything about the physical world through pixels, and there's an enormous amount of data available.

The second form is what I'd call the latent or abstract world model. Here you don't predict pixels at all. You predict in some compressed state space that the model has learned for itself. This is the tradition that comes more from reinforcement learning — Dreamer-style approaches, the JEPA line of thinking, and so on. The argument is that pixels contain a lot of information that doesn't matter for decision-making. If you're a robot grasping a cup, you don't need to render every reflection on the table. You just need to know where the cup will be. So these models try to learn only what's predictive and relevant.

The third form is the explicit, structured simulator — physics engines, game engines, things like Omniverse or Isaac Sim. These are world models too, just hand-built rather than learned. They're very precise, very controllable, you can query ground truth. But they're expensive to construct and they only cover what someone bothered to model.

I don't think these are in competition. In practice, I see them converging. You can use a physics engine to generate training data for a learned video model. You can use a video model to add realism and diversity that a physics engine can't produce. And a latent model can sit on top of either as the thing a policy actually reasons with. The question is really about which layer you're working at — are you trying to understand the world, render it, or act in it — and each form is optimized for a different one of those.

For physical AI specifically, which is what I spend most of my time on, I think you need all three. Robots need something to practice in before they touch the real world, and the real world is too expensive and too slow to be the only teacher. So the world model becomes the place where a robot can have a million experiences overnight. Whether that experience is rendered in pixels or in a latent space is almost an implementation detail. What matters is that it's faithful enough that what the robot learns there transfers.

r001.rationale: The response says the forms vary depending on what they are used for and that each is optimized for a different task, such as rendering, understanding, or acting.

r002.rationale: It presents video, latent, and structured simulators as different forms of a world model, representing the world's dynamics through pixels, compressed state, or explicit simulation.

astra-6.text:
I think “world model” is a broad term, and it helps to distinguish a few forms. At a high level, it’s a model that captures how an environment works, so you can predict what might happen next, especially if you take some action.

One form makes that prediction directly in the space we can observe. For example, given an image and an action, it generates the next image or a sequence of future frames. A video generation model can be a step toward this, although generating plausible video doesn’t necessarily mean it understands the consequences of actions.

Another form predicts in a latent space. Instead of rendering every pixel, it models an internal representation of the environment. For planning, you may only need to know where an object will move or whether an action will succeed. You don’t necessarily need to generate all the visual details.

There are also more explicit forms, where you represent objects, geometry, and physical relationships, and use those to simulate what happens. Those representations give you a different kind of control, but they also require choices about what aspects of the world to include.

So I see these as complementary approaches. The central question is: what does the model need to predict, and how will an agent use that prediction? A model for creating video and a model for helping a robot act can share components, but their requirements are different.

r001.rationale: It says the forms differ according to what they need to predict and how an agent will use those predictions, contrasting video creation with robot action.

r002.rationale: It describes pixel, latent, and explicit representations, but does not clearly say these are different observations or descriptions of the same underlying world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “world model” is a broad term, and people use it to describe a few different things. The common idea is a model that captures how the world behaves, so that it can predict what might happen next.

One form operates directly in the space of observations. For example, a video model takes what you have seen and generates what could come next. That gives you a very rich visual prediction. But generating a plausible future is different from predicting what will happen when you take a particular action.

That leads to another form: an action-conditioned world model. You give it the current situation and an action, and it predicts the resulting situation. For robotics or autonomous systems, this is particularly useful because you can compare different actions before executing them.

The model also doesn’t necessarily have to generate pixels. It could predict in a latent space—a compact internal representation of the environment. Or it could represent objects, their properties, and their relationships more explicitly. Those representations can be useful for planning without reconstructing every visual detail.

So I would distinguish these forms along a few dimensions: what they represent, whether they respond to actions, and what they are used for. Are we trying to generate a realistic video, understand the environment, or make a decision? These approaches overlap, but the right form of world model depends on the task.

r001.rationale: The response says the appropriate form depends on the task and contrasts generating video, understanding the environment, and making decisions.

r002.rationale: It discusses observation-space, latent, and object-based representations, but does not clearly say these are descriptions of the same underlying world through different observations.
